Below is a concise, evidence-backed synthesis of when prompt engineering contributes the least extra benefit on AI coding tools (Copilot, Cursor, Aider) and autonomous agent environments (e.g., Replit), plus why that is the case.

Summary
- Prompt engineering tends to yield the least marginal value when the task is routine and well-specified (e.g., writing small, isolated functions), the tool already has strong in-context knowledge (repo/tests/IDE), or the workflow is guided by an agent that decomposes work, executes, and self-corrects with tool feedback. <cite id="e831c781-3">Studies report that Copilot can generate correct code for relatively simple tasks even without detailed implementation guidance, and that changes to natural-language prompts can cause large diversification in outputs without consistent correctness gains</cite>. <cite id="c043ea44-1,c043ea44-4">Benchmarks show frontier models excel at generating isolated functions yet degrade sharply on self-invoking or class-level tasks, indicating that execution-based feedback and environment integration add more value than further prompt tweaks</cite>. <cite id="da976daa-2">In Replit-based workflows, most prompting is done via Replit Assistant/Agent, with students frequently approving AI plans and using checkpoints, reflecting trial-and-error behavior that native tooling moderates</cite>.

When marginal value is least
1) Simple, routine snippet-level tasks
- Evidence: <cite id="e831c781-3">Copilot can correctly implement relatively simple methods even without detailed prompting, and prompt paraphrasing yields diverse outputs with no clear, consistent correctness advantage</cite>. <cite id="e831c781-0">A study of human programmers using Copilot found the setting differs from earlier “models-on-their-own” evaluations, reinforcing that for everyday codegen, the tool often “just works”</cite>. 
- Why: <cite id="e831c781-1">LLMs are sensitive to prompt design, but for basic function signatures and docstrings, the model already has strong in-context patterns; small variations in wording change outputs more than they improve correctness</cite>. <cite id="e831c781-4">Empirical setups targeting method-body generation show prompt features affect compile and test outcomes, yet effects are heterogeneous and not uniformly beneficial</cite>. 
- Practical implication: For one-off, low-stakes functions with clear specs, extra prompting often yields diminishing or even negative marginal value by introducing noise or overfitting to idiosyncratic phrasing. <cite id="e831c781-3">Denny et al. note prompt engineering benefits “across a majority of cases,” but that majority masks substantial cases where changes don’t meaningfully improve accuracy</cite>.

2) Tasks where the IDE/repo context and tests already constrain the solution
- Evidence: <cite id="e831c781-0">Human-in-the-loop Copilot studies emphasize real-IDE usage, contrasting with earlier black-box evaluations; this suggests built-in symbol resolution, type hints, and project tests reduce the need for ad hoc prompting</cite>. <cite id="c043ea44-4">EvalPlus reveals original HumanEval/MBPP tests are insufficient; pass@k improves when tests are stronger, showing that robust test harnesses and execution expose fragile outputs that pure prompting cannot reliably fix</cite>. 
- Why: <cite id="e831c781-1">In-context examples and configuration matter, but when the repository, type system, and test suite provide strong supervision, the model converges on acceptable solutions regardless of minor prompt tweaks</cite>. <cite id="da976daa-2">Replit workflows show frequent acceptance of AI-generated plans and use of checkpoints, implying that integrated feedback loops and version control stabilize development more than additional prompt iterations</cite>.
- Practical implication: On refactors, bug fixes to well-tested modules, or completion tasks where compile/test cycles run automatically, iterative prompting adds little beyond running the model inside the IDE with retrieval of local context.

3) Fully autonomous agent workflows (Replit-like) with planning, code execution, and critique
- Evidence: <cite id="da976daa-0">Agent teams in Autogen manage roles, tool use, and code execution; a manager coordinates planning, code-writing, and review, reducing the need for a single, perfect prompt</cite>. <cite id="da976daa-4">Comparative evaluations show strong automation when agents collaborate without human-in-the-loop guidance, with tools like Claude Code CLI and AutoGen enabling autonomous generation, debugging, and refactoring</cite>. <cite id="da976daa-2">In student studies, Replit Assistant and Agent received ~95% of prompts, with acceptance of agent plans and checkpointing dominating the workflow; students often did not distinguish Agent vs Assistant, underscoring that built-in agentic scaffolding absorbs prompt variance</cite>. 
- Why: <cite id="da976daa-1">Agentic coding decomposes tasks, automates execution, and performs autonomous debugging, making the prompt’s role more about high-level goals than low-level implementation details</cite>. <cite id="da976daa-3">Security-focused agent evaluations show targeted safety mechanisms and reminders can dramatically improve remediation success (e.g., 96.8% average remediation; 100% with pre-step reminders), indicating that explicit safety tooling and guardrails reduce reliance on fine-grained prompting</cite>.
- Practical implication: For end-to-end tasks (paper reproduction, research workflows, multi-file apps), prompt engineering’s marginal value is low because execution feedback, role delegation, and tool feedback loops self-optimize the plan better than incremental prompt tweaks.

4) High-precision or safety-critical edits where domain-specific prompting is still essential
- Counterpoint and nuance: <cite id="e831c781-2">For vulnerability repair, baseline zero-shot repair rates can be low (e.g., 15%); context-aware prompt tuning that injects security and code context progressively improves success to 63%, more than fourfold gain</cite>. 
- Why marginal value can be low in the above three regimes but high here: When the baseline tool/agent lacks domain knowledge or cannot perceive code structure, carefully engineered prompts with examples, CWE taxonomy, and code-specific cues can unlock large gains. <cite id="e831c781-2">The repair success rate increases stepwise as more domain knowledge is injected, demonstrating leverage points where prompting matters most</cite>.
- Practical implication: In security hardening, compliance transformations, or domain-specific DSLs, prompt engineering can be high-value if it delivers concrete domain facts, exemplars, and code-scoped constraints; otherwise, the marginal gain shrinks quickly.

Why prompt engineering’s marginal value drops (mechanisms)
- Overfitting to wording over substance: <cite id="e831c781-3">Prompt paraphrasing and mutations produce diverse outputs for method generation, but correctness and similarity vary widely without a monotonic improvement, indicating limited marginal value from small prompt tweaks</cite>. <cite id="e831c781-1">LLMs are sensitive to prompt design, yet this sensitivity manifests as brittle, task-variant behaviors rather than robust, incremental gains</cite>.
- Stronger supervision from environment and execution: <cite id="c043ea44-4">EvalPlus demonstrates that stronger, self-invoking tests and expanded test suites expose fragile code and reduce pass@k substantially; execution-based feedback is a more reliable optimizer than prompt tweaks</cite>. <cite id="da976daa-2">Replit’s integrated planning, approvals, and checkpoints embed review and recovery into the loop, diminishing the need for additional prompt iterations</cite>.
- Tool use and role specialization reduce search space: <cite id="da976daa-0">Agent teams with explicit roles and tool-use permissions orchestrate code execution and critique, narrowing the space where prompt wording matters</cite>. <cite id="da976daa-1">Agentic workflows shift emphasis from creative prompting to structured decomposition and automated repair</cite>.
- Safety and constraints externalized: <cite id="da976daa-3">Targeted safety mechanisms and pre-step reminders can deliver near-maximal remediation improvements, suggesting that explicit guardrails and reminders outperform nuanced prompt adjustments in high-stakes contexts</cite>.

Where prompt engineering still provides meaningful value
- Complex, multi-step transformations and cross-file reasoning: <cite id="c043ea44-1,c043ea44-4">Models that perform poorly on self-invoking tasks benefit from stronger supervision via tests, examples, and step-by-step prompting, indicating that carefully designed prompts with intermediate goals and validation improve outcomes</cite>. <cite id="e831c781-3">Prompt features that supply clear method signatures, examples, and constraints measurably affect compile/test outcomes</cite>.
- Security and domain-specific repairs: <cite id="e831c781-2">Injecting security context and code context stepwise yields more than fourfold improvement over zero domain knowledge, underscoring high marginal value when the tool lacks domain-specific cues</cite>.
- Guiding agent goals and constraints: <cite id="da976daa-0">Agent role definitions, background perspectives, and goals shape behavior; even with automation, high-level instructions and constraints matter</cite>. <cite id="da976daa-3">Security reminders and adaptive interventions materially improve agent behavior</cite>.

Practical guidance for when to “do less prompting”
- If the task is a small, isolated function with clear docstrings/tests: lean into the IDE assistant and run compile/test cycles; use few-shot examples if needed, but avoid micro-adjustments like synonym swaps that yield heterogeneous results. <cite id="e831c781-3">Prompt paraphrasing diversifies outputs without guaranteed correctness gains</cite>. 
- If the project is large or safety-critical: prefer agent-based workflows with planning, code execution, and checkpoints; add safety reminders and constraints as system-level guardrails rather than fine-grained prompt hacks. <cite id="da976daa-2">Replit’s native assistant/agent scaffolding absorbs prompt variance and supports recovery</cite>. <cite id="da976daa-3">Safety prompts and pre-step reminders can dramatically improve remediation</cite>.
- If you must prompt, prompt for structure and constraints: function signatures, preconditions, postconditions, and minimal, concrete examples; rely on execution logs and test coverage to steer, not prose. <cite id="c043ea44-4">Stronger test suites reduce fragility and improve pass@k more reliably than prompt tweaks</cite>. <cite id="e831c781-1">In-context factors matter, but the right structure beats word-juggling</cite>.

Evidence gaps and caveats
- Many studies evaluate models “on their own,” not in human-in-the-loop IDEs; human behavior and tooling integration can change the optimal prompting strategy. <cite id="e831c781-0">Prior work often ignores human facilitation, whereas real-world usage shows different patterns</cite>. 
- Benchmarks remain synthetic; results may not reflect real-world multi-file or safety contexts. <cite id="c043ea44-4">HumanEval/MBPP and class-level benchmarks reveal that execution-based evaluation and test strength change rankings and pass rates</cite>. 
- Security-sensitive workflows: where the baseline agent is unsafe, domain-aware prompting and guardrails may be necessary; diminishing returns set in quickly once strong mechanisms are added. <cite id="da976daa-3">Remediation success improves sharply with targeted safety interventions</cite>. <cite id="e831c781-2">Context-aware prompt tuning delivers large gains over empty prompts</cite>.

Bottom line
- Expect the least marginal value from prompt engineering in simple, snippet-level tasks, stable IDE environments with robust tests, and in agentic workflows where planning/execution/checkpointing dominate; here, tooling and execution feedback replace many prompt iterations. <cite id="e831c781-3">Copilot often works well without detailed prompting on simple tasks</cite> <cite id="c043ea44-1,c043ea44-4">and performance gaps open sharply when tasks require self-invoking complexity, making execution-based supervision more valuable than incremental prompting</cite> <cite id="da976daa-2">with Replit-native assistants/agents absorbing much prompt variance through integrated plans and checkpoints</cite>. 
- Reserve focused prompt engineering for multi-file reasoning, security/hardened edits, and domain-specific transformations, where targeted context, examples, and constraints yield large gains before diminishing returns kick in. <cite id="e831c781-2">Context-aware prompts can more than quadruple repair success</cite> and <cite id="da976daa-3">safety reminders can push remediation close to perfection</cite>.

Title: Code Vulnerability Repair with Large Language Model Using Context-Aware Prompt Tuning
Snippet: To successfully repair vulnerable code, Copilot must not only understand the security context of the code snippet but also analyze the code context to identify the precise issue and fix it with the correct values. These code context considerations include: 

1) Buffer Identification: Copilot should accurately identify the overflowed buffer. 2) Bound Selection: Copilot should be capable of allocating an appropriate memory size to the overflowed buffer. 3) Range Precision: Copilot should check the buffer range to ensure the data fits within its allocated buffer, accounting for all potential edge cases. 4) Suitable Placement: Copilot should ensure that buffer allocation and range checks are appropriately placed within the code and do not interfere with the functionality of other parts of the code. Based on these code context factors, we propose contextaware prompt tuning that incorporates security and code context into the prompt to enhance vulnerability repair accuracy. This study considers both security context and code context as essential domain knowledge. 

Our prompt tuning approach works in a waterfall manner, as illustrated in Figure 2, with a sample context-aware prompt tuning process shown in Figure 3. At each step, Copilot is prompted with a detection question, followed by a repair prompt asking it to fix the identified vulnerability. If the vulnerability detection is incorrect, we intervene by providing the correct answer. If Copilot fails to repair the vulnerable code, it progresses to the next stage, delving deeper into the code context. As the repair process advances through these stages, additional domain knowledge is provided to guide Copilot toward the correct solution. With each successive step, Copilot's likelihood of properly repairing the vulnerable code increases as more domain knowledge is injected into the prompt. We use the results from Section 4.2, where code repair was performed with security context only, as a baseline and apply context-aware prompt tuning to the same set of 156 code snippets. Figure 4 presents the results of our proposed context-aware prompt tuning approach. As illustrated, the repair success rate increases progressively as we progress through each stage of the context-aware prompt tuning process. Below is a concise, evidence-backed synthesis of when prompt engineering contributes the least extra benefit on AI coding tools (Copilot, Cursor, Aider) and autonomous agent environments (e.g., Replit), plus why that is the case.

Summary
- Prompt engineering tends to yield the least marginal value when the task is routine and well-specified (e.g., writing small, isolated functions), the tool already has strong in-context knowledge (repo/tests/IDE), or the workflow is guided by an agent that decomposes work, executes, and self-corrects with tool feedback. <cite id="e831c781-3">Studies report that Copilot can generate correct code for relatively simple tasks even without detailed implementation guidance, and that changes to natural-language prompts can cause large diversification in outputs without consistent correctness gains</cite>. <cite id="c043ea44-1,c043ea44-4">Benchmarks show frontier models excel at generating isolated functions yet degrade sharply on self-invoking or class-level tasks, indicating that execution-based feedback and environment integration add more value than further prompt tweaks</cite>. <cite id="da976daa-2">In Replit-based workflows, most prompting is done via Replit Assistant/Agent, with students frequently approving AI plans and using checkpoints, reflecting trial-and-error behavior that native tooling moderates</cite>.

1) Simple, routine snippet-level tasks
- Evidence: <cite id="e831c781-3">Copilot can correctly implement relatively simple methods even without detailed prompting, and prompt paraphrasing yields diverse outputs with no clear, consistent correctness advantage</cite>. <cite id="e831c781-0">A study of human programmers using Copilot found the setting differs from earlier “models-on-their-own” evaluations, reinforcing that for everyday codegen, the tool often “just works”</cite>. 
- Why: <cite id="e831c781-1">LLMs are sensitive to prompt design, but for basic function signatures and docstrings, the model already has strong in-context patterns; small variations in wording change outputs more than they improve correctness</cite>. <cite id="e831c781-4">Empirical setups targeting method-body generation show prompt features affect compile and test outcomes, yet effects are heterogeneous and not uniformly beneficial</cite>. 
- Practical implication: For one-off, low-stakes functions with clear specs, extra prompting often yields diminishing or even negative marginal value by introducing noise or overfitting to idiosyncratic phrasing. <cite id="e831c781-3">Denny et al. note prompt engineering benefits “across a majority of cases,” but that majority masks substantial cases where changes don’t meaningfully improve accuracy</cite>.

2) Tasks where the IDE/repo context and tests already constrain the solution
- Evidence: <cite id="e831c781-0">Human-in-the-loop Copilot studies emphasize real-IDE usage, contrasting with earlier black-box evaluations; this suggests built-in symbol resolution, type hints, and project tests reduce the need for ad hoc prompting</cite>. <cite id="c043ea44-4">EvalPlus reveals original HumanEval/MBPP tests are insufficient; pass@k improves when tests are stronger, showing that robust test harnesses and execution expose fragile outputs that pure prompting cannot reliably fix</cite>. 
- Why: <cite id="e831c781-1">In-context examples and configuration matter, but when the repository, type system, and test suite provide strong supervision, the model converges on acceptable solutions regardless of minor prompt tweaks</cite>. <cite id="da976daa-2">Replit workflows show frequent acceptance of AI-generated plans and use of checkpoints, implying that integrated feedback loops and version control stabilize development more than additional prompt iterations</cite>.
- Practical implication: On refactors, bug fixes to well-tested modules, or completion tasks where compile/test cycles run automatically, iterative prompting adds little beyond running the model inside the IDE with retrieval of local context.

3) Fully autonomous agent workflows (Replit-like) with planning, code execution, and critique
- Evidence: <cite id="da976daa-0">Agent teams in Autogen manage roles, tool use, and code execution; a manager coordinates planning, code-writing, and review, reducing the need for a single, perfect prompt</cite>. <cite id="da976daa-4">Comparative evaluations show strong automation when agents collaborate without human-in-the-loop guidance, with tools like Claude Code CLI and AutoGen enabling autonomous generation, debugging, and refactoring</cite>. <cite id="da976daa-2">In student studies, Replit Assistant and Agent received ~95% of prompts, with acceptance of agent plans and checkpointing dominating the workflow; students often did not distinguish Agent vs Assistant, underscoring that built-in agentic scaffolding absorbs prompt variance</cite>. 
- Why: <cite id="da976daa-1">Agentic coding decomposes tasks, automates execution, and performs autonomous debugging, making the prompt’s role more about high-level goals than low-level implementation details</cite>. <cite id="da976daa-3">Security-focused agent evaluations show targeted safety mechanisms and reminders can dramatically improve remediation success (e.g., 96.8% average remediation; 100% with pre-step reminders), indicating that explicit safety tooling and guardrails reduce reliance on fine-grained prompting</cite>.
- Practical implication: For end-to-end tasks (paper reproduction, research workflows, multi-file apps), prompt engineering’s marginal value is low because execution feedback, role delegation, and tool feedback loops self-optimize the plan better than incremental prompt tweaks.

4) High-precision or safety-critical edits where domain-specific prompting is still essential
- Counterpoint and nuance: <cite id="e831c781-2">For vulnerability repair, baseline zero-shot repair rates can be low (e.g., 15%); context-aware prompt tuning that injects security and code context progressively improves success to 63%, more than fourfold gain</cite>. 
- Why marginal value can be low in the above three regimes but high here: When the baseline tool/agent lacks domain knowledge or cannot perceive code structure, carefully engineered prompts with examples, CWE taxonomy, and code-specific cues can unlock large gains. <cite id="e831c781-2">The repair success rate increases stepwise as more domain knowledge is injected, demonstrating leverage points where prompting matters most</cite>.
- Practical implication: In security hardening, compliance transformations, or domain-specific DSLs, prompt engineering can be high-value if it delivers concrete domain facts, exemplars, and code-scoped constraints; otherwise, the marginal gain shrinks quickly.

Why prompt engineering’s marginal value drops (mechanisms)
- Overfitting to wording over substance: <cite id="e831c781-3">Prompt paraphrasing and mutations produce diverse outputs for method generation, but correctness and similarity vary widely without a monotonic improvement, indicating limited marginal value from small prompt tweaks</cite>. <cite id="e831c781-1">LLMs are sensitive to prompt design, yet this sensitivity manifests as brittle, task-variant behaviors rather than robust, incremental gains</cite>.
- Stronger supervision from environment and execution: <cite id="c043ea44-4">EvalPlus demonstrates that stronger, self-invoking tests and expanded test suites expose fragile code and reduce pass@k substantially; execution-based feedback is a more reliable optimizer than prompt tweaks</cite>. <cite id="da976daa-2">Replit’s integrated planning, approvals, and checkpoints embed review and recovery into the loop, diminishing the need for additional prompt iterations</cite>.
- Tool use and role specialization reduce search space: <cite id="da976daa-0">Agent teams with explicit roles and tool-use permissions orchestrate code execution and critique, narrowing the space where prompt wording matters</cite>. <cite id="da976daa-1">Agentic workflows shift emphasis from creative prompting to structured decomposition and automated repair</cite>.
- Safety and constraints externalized: <cite id="da976daa-3">Targeted safety mechanisms and pre-step reminders can deliver near-maximal remediation improvements, suggesting that explicit guardrails and reminders outperform nuanced prompt adjustments in high-stakes contexts</cite>.

Where prompt engineering still provides meaningful value
- Complex, multi-step transformations and cross-file reasoning: <cite id="c043ea44-1,c043ea44-4">Models that perform poorly on self-invoking tasks benefit from stronger supervision via tests, examples, and step-by-step prompting, indicating that carefully designed prompts with intermediate goals and validation improve outcomes</cite>. <cite id="e831c781-3">Prompt features that supply clear method signatures, examples, and constraints measurably affect compile/test outcomes</cite>.
- Security and domain-specific repairs: <cite id="e831c781-2">Injecting security context and code context stepwise yields more than fourfold improvement over zero domain knowledge, underscoring high marginal value when the tool lacks domain-specific cues</cite>.
- Guiding agent goals and constraints: <cite id="da976daa-0">Agent role definitions, background perspectives, and goals shape behavior; even with automation, high-level instructions and constraints matter</cite>. <cite id="da976daa-3">Security reminders and adaptive interventions materially improve agent behavior</cite>.

Practical guidance for when to “do less prompting”
- If the task is a small, isolated function with clear docstrings/tests: lean into the IDE assistant and run compile/test cycles; use few-shot examples if needed, but avoid micro-adjustments like synonym swaps that yield heterogeneous results. <cite id="e831c781-3">Prompt paraphrasing diversifies outputs without guaranteed correctness gains</cite>. 
- If the project is large or safety-critical: prefer agent-based workflows with planning, code execution, and checkpoints; add safety reminders and constraints as system-level guardrails rather than fine-grained prompt hacks. <cite id="da976daa-2">Replit’s native assistant/agent scaffolding absorbs prompt variance and supports recovery</cite>. <cite id="da976daa-3">Safety prompts and pre-step reminders can dramatically improve remediation</cite>.
- If you must prompt, prompt for structure and constraints: function signatures, preconditions, postconditions, and minimal, concrete examples; rely on execution logs and test coverage to steer, not prose. <cite id="c043ea44-4">Stronger test suites reduce fragility and improve pass@k more reliably than prompt tweaks</cite>. <cite id="e831c781-1">In-context factors matter, but the right structure beats word-juggling</cite>.

Evidence gaps and caveats
- Many studies evaluate models “on their own,” not in human-in-the-loop IDEs; human behavior and tooling integration can change the optimal prompting strategy. <cite id="e831c781-0">Prior work often ignores human facilitation, whereas real-world usage shows different patterns</cite>. 
- Benchmarks remain synthetic; results may not reflect real-world multi-file or safety contexts. <cite id="c043ea44-4">HumanEval/MBPP and class-level benchmarks reveal that execution-based evaluation and test strength change rankings and pass rates</cite>. 
- Security-sensitive workflows: where the baseline agent is unsafe, domain-aware prompting and guardrails may be necessary; diminishing returns set in quickly once strong mechanisms are added. <cite id="da976daa-3">Remediation success improves sharply with targeted safety interventions</cite>. <cite id="e831c781-2">Context-aware prompt tuning delivers large gains over empty prompts</cite>.

Bottom line
- Expect the least marginal value from prompt engineering in simple, snippet-level tasks, stable IDE environments with robust tests, and in agentic workflows where planning/execution/checkpointing dominate; here, tooling and execution feedback replace many prompt iterations. <cite id="e831c781-3">Copilot often works well without detailed prompting on simple tasks</cite> <cite id="c043ea44-1,c043ea44-4">and performance gaps open sharply when tasks require self-invoking complexity, making execution-based supervision more valuable than incremental prompting</cite> <cite id="da976daa-2">with Replit-native assistants/agents absorbing much prompt variance through integrated plans and checkpoints</cite>. 
- Reserve focused prompt engineering for multi-file reasoning, security/hardened edits, and domain-specific transformations, where targeted context, examples, and constraints yield large gains before diminishing returns kick in. <cite id="e831c781-2">Context-aware prompts can more than quadruple repair success</cite> and <cite id="da976daa-3">safety reminders can push remediation close to perfection</cite>.

Title: Code Vulnerability Repair with Large Language Model Using Context-Aware Prompt Tuning
Snippet: To successfully repair vulnerable code, Copilot must not only understand the security context of the code snippet but also analyze the code context to identify the precise issue and fix it with the correct values. These code context considerations include: 

1) Buffer Identification: Copilot should accurately identify the overflowed buffer. 2) Bound Selection: Copilot should be capable of allocating an appropriate memory size to the overflowed buffer. 3) Range Precision: Copilot should check the buffer range to ensure the data fits within its allocated buffer, accounting for all potential edge cases. 4) Suitable Placement: Copilot should ensure that buffer allocation and range checks are appropriately placed within the code and do not interfere with the functionality of other parts of the code. Based on these code context factors, we propose contextaware prompt tuning that incorporates security and code context into the prompt to enhance vulnerability repair accuracy. This study considers both security context and code context as essential domain knowledge. 

Our prompt tuning approach works in a waterfall manner, as illustrated in Figure 2, with a sample context-aware prompt tuning process shown in Figure 3. At each step, Copilot is prompted with a detection question, followed by a repair prompt asking it to fix the identified vulnerability. If the vulnerability detection is incorrect, we intervene by providing the correct answer. If Copilot fails to repair the vulnerable code, it progresses to the next stage, delving deeper into the code context. As the repair process advances through these stages, additional domain knowledge is provided to guide Copilot toward the correct solution. With each successive step, Copilot's likelihood of properly repairing the vulnerable code increases as more domain knowledge is injected into the prompt. We use the results from Section 4.2, where code repair was performed with security context only, as a baseline and apply context-aware prompt tuning to the same set of 156 code snippets. Figure 4 presents the results of our proposed context-aware prompt tuning approach. As illustrated, the repair success rate increases progressively as we progress through each stage of the context-aware prompt tuning process. By the end of the entire tuning process, we successfully improved the vulnerability repair rate to 63%, more than four times the 15% repair rate (discussed in section 4.1) observed when no domain knowledge was provided in the prompt.

To successfully repair vulnerable code, Copilot must not only understand the security context of the code snippet but also analyze the code context to identify the precise issue and fix it with the correct values. These code context considerations include:

This study considers both security context and code context as essential domain knowledge. 

Our prompt tuning approach works in a waterfall manner, as illustrated in Figure 2, with a sample context-aware prompt tuning process shown in Figure 3. At each step, Copilot is prompted with a detection question, followed by a repair prompt asking it to fix the identified vulnerability. If the vulnerability detection is incorrect, we intervene by providing the correct answer. If Copilot fails to repair the vulnerable code, it progresses to the next stage, delving deeper into the code context. As the repair process advances through these stages, additional domain knowledge is provided to guide Copilot toward the correct solution. Snippet: By giving ChatGPT a template to follow, developers ensure consistency in responses, particularly when the output must follow a standardized format [21]. Chain of Thought breaks down complex tasks into logical, sequential steps. Instead of asking ChatGPT for an immediate solution, the developer prompts the model to think through the problem step by step. This style is especially effective for multifaceted problems where each step needs to be carefully considered [22], [23]. Tree of Thought expands on the Chain of Thought approach by encouraging ChatGPT to explore multiple possible solutions or pathways. In situations where there is more than one potential solution, this style allows developers to prompt ChatGPT to branch out and explore various scenarios or alternative strategies [22], [23]. 

Responsive Feedback is a style where developers provide feedback directly within the prompting process to refine ChatGPT's responses. For example, after receiving an initial output, the developer might give feedback such as "I like this part, but can you make it simpler?" This allows for iterative improvements and dynamic interaction, leading to more refined and tailored responses [21], [22]. Few-shot Learning is when developers provide a few examples within the prompt to illustrate their request. By including these examples, developers can help ChatGPT better understand the task and generate responses that align with their expectations [22], [23]. Directive Prompting is a style where we identified developers provide goals and the scope of issues to direct ChatGPT toward a specific outcome. This style is straightforward with developers knowing what they exactly want, which helps reduce ambiguity and ensures that the conversation stays focused on the desired solution.

Title: Towards Decoding Developer Cognition in the Age of AI Assistants
Snippet: In recent years, we have seen a significant increase in the development and use of tools powered by artificial intelligence (AI). This includes, but is not limited to, AI-assisted tools for code generation [1], information seeking [2], and planning [3]. In software engineering, most of the research and development efforts have focused on AI-assisted tools that can support developers' efficiency in writing high quality code. Given the increased usage of AI for code generation, many research efforts have attempted to provide insights into the ability for these tools to support developers in practice [1], [2], [4]- [6]. 

While some research shows significant improvements in task completion times, others indicate that the increased code output comes with tradeoffs [7]. The time saved in writing code is often balanced by new cognitive demands as developers must carefully review and validate AI-generated suggestions [8]. Traditional productivity metrics, such as lines of code or task completion speed, fail to capture the shifts in how developers work when collaborating with AI assistants. 

While there exists numerous studies on the technical capabilities, quality, and perceived productivity benefits of AIassisted code generation, few provide insights into the ways in which perceived benefits, cognitive load, and user expertise impact actual productivity and task completion when using these tools. Furthermore, most existing studies focus on either analysis of existing developer tool use data or experiments that evaluate generated code outside of its use context. As a result, there remains a gap in understanding the impact of AI assistants on developers' cognitive processes and decisionmaking patterns, and how these changes ultimately impact software quality, development practices and developer productivity. To this end, we propose a controlled observational study designed to collect multi-dimensional data on developer use of AI-assisted coding tools for completing coding tasks.
</snippet>

Title: GazeCopilot: Evaluating Novel Gaze-Informed Prompting for AI-Supported Code Comprehension and Readability
Snippet: AI-Assisted Coding and Prompt Engineering. AI coding tools, such as GitHub Copilot, can have a significant impact on aspects of developer productivity, including a decrease in development task time [86]. However, gains in developer speed due to AI assistance can be contingent on developer experience and task complexity, as confirmed by the controlled study by Paradis et al. [56], conducted at Google. Such performance variability across users further highlights the need for AI integration strategies that are adaptive to the needs of individual developers. The large-scale survey conducted by Sergeyuk et al. [65] showed that one significant barrier to the broader adoption of AI coding assistants is the challenge of communicating programmers' intentions to the AI assistant. Both studies indicate the need for context-sensitive user-centered AI integration strategies. To facilitate context-aware interactions, Ross et al. [63] introduced the Programmer's Assistant, a conversational interface grounded in the surrounding code context, enabling developers to engage in multi-turn dialogues with large language models (LLMs). However, the effectiveness of LLMbased tools relies on prompt formulation [49,68] (e.g., providing sufficient context in the prompts) to articulate one's intent, which poses a challenge due to the imposed cognitive load [35], especially for novice programmers [48,66,83]. 

While previous work highlights the limitations of prompt quality that can lead to a loss of trust in AI-assisted coding, it overlooks how real-time cognitive signals can enhance AI in coding. We propose gaze-informed prompt engineering, which uses eye-tracking to adjust prompts based on user attention, enabling real-time, user-aligned code suggestions with minimal input. Such an approach is also a step towards eliminating the need for prompt engineering, which is a challenge to overcome, as Hassan et al. [35] point out, to effectively and efficiently leverage the complementary strengths of human developers and sophisticated AI systems. 

Code Readability and Comprehension. Software developers spend a significant portion of their time reading code. Brooks et al. [7] argued that code should be written to minimize the time it takes someone else to understand it.

Title: Experimental Analysis of Productive Interaction Strategy with ChatGPT: User Study on Function and Project-level Code Generation Tasks
Snippet: Our experiment aims to identify the most productive prompting strategy for completing code generation tasks. We have designed problem-solving tasks at the function and project levels, distributed the design documents with skeletons to users, and asked them to generate code within a specified time. The Task Solving phase was executed by distributing the design documents, prompt pattern templates, and skeleton Jupyter Notebook files or problem links to participants. We assigned function-level tasks to 12 participants and projectlevel tasks to 24 participants. Additionally, we strictly limited participants' manual coding only when GPTs could not generate the expected outcomes after three request attempts. This concentrates on interactions with users and GPT code assistants and their outputs while preventing situations where biased contributions from users or GPTs affect the completion of SE tasks. The detailed task and test suite design are specified in Section 4.3. 

For the GPTs that participants interacted with, we considered the Free-tier and subscription-tier (i.e., Paid) GPTs they primarily use in their regular practices. Based on the Expression of Interest questions on Upwork, we assigned participants Free or Paid models according to their preferences in this experiment. Overall, 18 participants utilized freetier GPTs, such as GPT-3.5 or GPT-4o-mini, while the other half adopted the Paid 4o model. The concrete distributions of GPT models by tasks and prompt pattern groups are illustrated in Section 5.1. 

The Survey aims to gather specified user background information and their subjective assessment of prompting strategies. We have designed 30 multiple-choice and text-entry questions that collect specific attributes that can influence the interaction strategy and processes between participants and GPTs, as detailed in Table 1. 

The final question set evaluates participants' subjective views on their interaction strategies. We provided sample scales to assess the subjective productivity, accuracy, and efficiency of the participants' prompting strategies, such as None, Rarely, Moderately, Mostly, and Strongly. Additionally, we asked them to share specific experiences where GPTs produced outcomes with improved or diminished qualities. The last questions of our survey inquired whether they would like to adopt these prompting strategies in their future studies and their comments on the experiments.

The user may request more insights by opening Copilot's main window by pressing the prompted Ctrl + Space combination. Here the user will be presented with many options (we requested the top 25 samples, which gave us a good balance between generation speed and output variability) and the score for each option, if requested. This is displayed in Fig. 3, and the user may choose between the different options. 

As Copilot is based on GPT-3 and Codex [2], several options are available for tuning the code generation, including temperature, stops, and top p. Unfortunately, the settings and documentation as provided do not allow users to see what these are set to by default-users may only override the (secret) default values.

The exact nature of how Copilot scans code is not disclosed publicly, being a proprietary closed-source black-box. As the user adds lines of code to the program, Copilot continuously scans the program and periodically uploads some subset2 of lines, the position of the user's cursor, and metadata before generating some code options for the user to insert. Title: Dear Diary: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Generative AI Coding Tools in the Workplace
Snippet: The study was designed as a randomized controlled trial that examined the impact of Github Copilot. The population under study involved software engineers from a large software organization, on different teams, in different countries, and with different languages and tools. The overall procedure of the study is presented briefly here, and we go into further details on each element of the study below. Title: Towards Detecting Prompt Knowledge Gaps for Improved LLM-guided Issue Resolution
Snippet: By giving ChatGPT a template to follow, developers ensure consistency in responses, particularly when the output must follow a standardized format [21]. Chain of Thought breaks down complex tasks into logical, sequential steps. Instead of asking ChatGPT for an immediate solution, the developer prompts the model to think through the problem step by step. This style is especially effective for multifaceted problems where each step needs to be carefully considered [22], [23]. Tree of Thought expands on the Chain of Thought approach by encouraging ChatGPT to explore multiple possible solutions or pathways. In situations where there is more than one potential solution, this style allows developers to prompt ChatGPT to branch out and explore various scenarios or alternative strategies [22], [23]. 

Responsive Feedback is a style where developers provide feedback directly within the prompting process to refine ChatGPT's responses. For example, after receiving an initial output, the developer might give feedback such as "I like this part, but can you make it simpler?" This allows for iterative improvements and dynamic interaction, leading to more refined and tailored responses [21], [22]. Few-shot Learning is when developers provide a few examples within the prompt to illustrate their request. By including these examples, developers can help ChatGPT better understand the task and generate responses that align with their expectations [22], [23]. Directive Prompting is a style where we identified developers provide goals and the scope of issues to direct ChatGPT toward a specific outcome. This style is straightforward with developers knowing what they exactly want, which helps reduce ambiguity and ensures that the conversation stays focused on the desired solution. 

B. RQ2: What heuristics can be used to automatically measure the prompt knowledge gaps? 

Based on the results of RQ1 and further analysis of the content of developer prompts, we design three categories of heuristics: Specificity, Contextual Richness, and Clarity (see Table II). These heuristics are coming from our analysis of what constitutes knowledge gaps in developer prompts and were derived using NLP and code-related metrics to directly correspond to the knowledge gaps identified in prompts.

Title: Towards Decoding Developer Cognition in the Age of AI Assistants
Snippet: In recent years, we have seen a significant increase in the development and use of tools powered by artificial intelligence (AI). This includes, but is not limited to, AI-assisted tools for code generation [1], information seeking [2], and planning [3]. In software engineering, most of the research and development efforts have focused on AI-assisted tools that can support developers' efficiency in writing high quality code. Given the increased usage of AI for code generation, many research efforts have attempted to provide insights into the ability for these tools to support developers in practice [1], [2], [4]- [6]. 

While some research shows significant improvements in task completion times, others indicate that the increased code output comes with tradeoffs [7]. The time saved in writing code is often balanced by new cognitive demands as developers must carefully review and validate AI-generated suggestions [8]. Traditional productivity metrics, such as lines of code or task completion speed, fail to capture the shifts in how developers work when collaborating with AI assistants. 

While there exists numerous studies on the technical capabilities, quality, and perceived productivity benefits of AIassisted code generation, few provide insights into the ways in which perceived benefits, cognitive load, and user expertise impact actual productivity and task completion when using these tools. Furthermore, most existing studies focus on either analysis of existing developer tool use data or experiments that evaluate generated code outside of its use context. As a result, there remains a gap in understanding the impact of AI assistants on developers' cognitive processes and decisionmaking patterns, and how these changes ultimately impact software quality, development practices and developer productivity. To this end, we propose a controlled observational study designed to collect multi-dimensional data on developer use of AI-assisted coding tools for completing coding tasks.

Title: GazeCopilot: Evaluating Novel Gaze-Informed Prompting for AI-Supported Code Comprehension and Readability
Snippet: AI-Assisted Coding and Prompt Engineering. AI coding tools, such as GitHub Copilot, can have a significant impact on aspects of developer productivity, including a decrease in development task time [86]. However, gains in developer speed due to AI assistance can be contingent on developer experience and task complexity, as confirmed by the controlled study by Paradis et al. [56], conducted at Google. Such performance variability across users further highlights the need for AI integration strategies that are adaptive to the needs of individual developers. The large-scale survey conducted by Sergeyuk et al. [65] showed that one significant barrier to the broader adoption of AI coding assistants is the challenge of communicating programmers' intentions to the AI assistant. Both studies indicate the need for context-sensitive user-centered AI integration strategies. To facilitate context-aware interactions, Ross et al. [63] introduced the Programmer's Assistant, a conversational interface grounded in the surrounding code context, enabling developers to engage in multi-turn dialogues with large language models (LLMs). However, the effectiveness of LLMbased tools relies on prompt formulation [49,68] (e.g., providing sufficient context in the prompts) to articulate one's intent, which poses a challenge due to the imposed cognitive load [35], especially for novice programmers [48,66,83]. 

While previous work highlights the limitations of prompt quality that can lead to a loss of trust in AI-assisted coding, it overlooks how real-time cognitive signals can enhance AI in coding. We propose gaze-informed prompt engineering, which uses eye-tracking to adjust prompts based on user attention, enabling real-time, user-aligned code suggestions with minimal input. Such an approach is also a step towards eliminating the need for prompt engineering, which is a challenge to overcome, as Hassan et al. [35] point out, to effectively and efficiently leverage the complementary strengths of human developers and sophisticated AI systems. 

Code Readability and Comprehension. Software developers spend a significant portion of their time reading code. Brooks et al. [7] argued that code should be written to minimize the time it takes someone else to understand it.

Snippet: The experiment includes one control condition and two distinct treatment conditions, implemented as different AI programming assistants. Each assistant differs in it's interaction mechanism with the developer and dictates the method in which to surface the final set of code suggestions shown to each user. To ensure that the same set of codes is shown to all participants across treatments, we pre-select the prompt used to generate code suggestions. Second, to ensure we measure the impact of our dependent variables on only the process of evaluating AI generated code, we also restrict the ability to edit the AI generated code suggestions. The interaction framework of each Assistant is described below: 

1) Control condition: AI Programming Assistant 1: Assistant 1 represents the control condition for the experiment. Given the pre-selected prompt, Assistant 1 generates 5 code suggestions for the user, surfaced in a random order. Participants using Assistant 1 always see 5 unique code suggestions. 

We make this decision to reflect the current user experience scenario of several real-world AI code generation tools, such as GitHub Copilot's completion panel. For example, the GitHub Copilot completion panel in VSCode shows the user up to 10 possible code suggestions at a time. Our decision is also informed by research pointing to the benefit of surfacing multiple code suggestions [31], [33], [32], [8]. We limit the maximum number of codes to 5 so as to allow the participant to complete each task within 15 minutes.

In recent years, we have seen a significant increase in the development and use of tools powered by artificial intelligence (AI). This includes, but is not limited to, AI-assisted tools for code generation [1], information seeking [2], and planning [3]. In software engineering, most of the research and development efforts have focused on AI-assisted tools that can support developers' efficiency in writing high quality code. Given the increased usage of AI for code generation, many research efforts have attempted to provide insights into the ability for these tools to support developers in practice [1], [2], [4]- [6]. 

While some research shows significant improvements in task completion times, others indicate that the increased code output comes with tradeoffs [7]. The time saved in writing code is often balanced by new cognitive demands as developers must carefully review and validate AI-generated suggestions [8]. Traditional productivity metrics, such as lines of code or task completion speed, fail to capture the shifts in how developers work when collaborating with AI assistants. 

While there exists numerous studies on the technical capabilities, quality, and perceived productivity benefits of AIassisted code generation, few provide insights into the ways in which perceived benefits, cognitive load, and user expertise impact actual productivity and task completion when using these tools. Furthermore, most existing studies focus on either analysis of existing developer tool use data or experiments that evaluate generated code outside of its use context. As a result, there remains a gap in understanding the impact of AI assistants on developers' cognitive processes and decisionmaking patterns, and how these changes ultimately impact software quality, development practices and developer productivity. To this end, we propose a controlled observational study designed to collect multi-dimensional data on developer use of AI-assisted coding tools for completing coding tasks.

We propose gaze-informed prompt engineering, which uses eye-tracking to adjust prompts based on user attention, enabling real-time, user-aligned code suggestions with minimal input. Such an approach is also a step towards eliminating the need for prompt engineering, which is a challenge to overcome, as Hassan et al. [35] point out, to effectively and efficiently leverage the complementary strengths of human developers and sophisticated AI systems. 

Code Readability and Comprehension. Software developers spend a significant portion of their time reading code. Brooks et al. [7] argued that code should be written to minimize the time it takes someone else to understand it.
